Coal shortage 
*23.  MISS MABEL REBELLO:  
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the country would head towards a 
severe coal shortage and the demand supply gap is likely to be widen 
from 55 million tonnes by the end of Tenth Plan (2006-07) to about 95 
million tonnes at the end of Eleventh Five Year Plan period; 
(b) whether this would require doubling of coal production to meet the 
projected demand; 
(c) if so, details of the action plan in this regard; and 
(d) whether Government propose to in volve private sector in coal mining 
to bridge this gap? 
THE MINISTER OF COAL (SHRI KARIYA MUNDA): (a) and (b) The 
Planning Commission has projected that against the estimated demand for coal 
by the end of the Tenth Plan (200607) of 460.50 million tonnes (M.T.) the 
domestic supply of coal will be of the order of 405 M.T which is likely to result in a 
demand supply gap of the order of 55 M.T. In respect of the projections for the 
end of the Eleventh Five Year Plan (201112) the Working Gr oup on Coal and 
Lignite in its report for the Tenth Plan has estimated a demand of 620 M.T. and 
domestic production of 525 M.T. which is likely to result in a demand supply gap 
of the order of 95 M.T. 
The estimated demand supply gap of 55  M.T. in the terminal year of the 
Tenth Plan (2006-07) is likely to be met through import of coal (estimated at 
34 M.T.) and also increasing the domestic coal pr oduction.The estimated 
demand supply gap by the end of the terminal 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2003] 
year of the Eleventh Five Year Plan is also likely to be met by increased import of 
coal increasing domestic production and also having an efficient demand 
management system in place. 
(c) In order to achieve the producti on targets set for the terminal year 
of the Tenth Plan (2006-07) the Coal companies have an action plan 
approved by the Planning Commission for incurring capital expenditure of 
the order of Rs. 16,423 Crore (including Rs. 14,310 Crore by Coal India 
Ltd. and Rs.2113CrorebySingareni Collieries Company Ltd). The Coal 
Production target in 2006-07 has been set at 405 M.T. which comprises 
350 M.T. from CIL and 36.13 M.T. from SCCL, and the remaining 18.87 
from private players including capt ive block holders. Of the envisaged 
total production of 386.13 M.T. from CIL and SCCL, CIL has identified 92 
new projects which will be taken up during the Tenth Plan which will 
contribute about 79.11 M.T. SCCL will implement 17 new projects for a 
capacity of 4.13 M.T. In addition to th is a number of steps are being taken 
to increase productivity from existing mines which include inter-alia. 
(i) Increase in mechanisation through introduction of continuous miners, 
longwall powered supports in underground mines, planning open cast 
mines with higher capacity excavators; 
(ii) Scheduled equipment maintenance programmes, utilisation of skilled 
manpower and also training personnel to handle capital intensive 
equipment, offloading certain activities such as overburden removal, 
mechanisation of Underground Mine operations and also opting for 
higher capacity HEMM. 
(d) The private sector is already allowed captive mining of coal for 
production of iron and steel. In addition to this, with effect from 9.6.1993, 
the Government has also allowed the private sector to captively mine 
coal for generation of power, washing of coal obtained from a mine or for 
other end uses as may be notified by the Government from time to 
time. Mining of Coal for production of cement has also been permitted 
by the Government vide notification dated 15-3-1996  Furthermore, 
the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Bill, 2000 has been 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 244-2000 which seeks to allow the 
private sector Indian companies to commercially mine coal and lignite 
without the existing restriction of captive consumption and also engage 
in exploration of coal and lignite re sources in the country. This Bill is 
presently under consideration in Parliament.

(i)  Article 356 should be used most sparingly, as a measure of last 
resort.

forces in a State.

I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (c) Keeping in view the overall dimensions of the left wing 
extremism, a Coordination Centre headed by the Union Home Secretary with Chief 
Secretaries and Directors General of Police of the seriously affected States, as

approach to tackle the problem of left wing extremism by removing all the 
shortcomings in intelligence gathering and sharing and for mounting well

(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The Governme nt has launched Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) for strengthening Sub-
Transmission and Distribution and improve financial viability of the States 
APDRP has the following two components: 
(i) Investment component-Government of India provides financial 
assistance to the States as additional Central Assistance over the 
above the normal Central Plan allocation, for strengthening and 
upgradation of sub-transmission and distribution network. APDRP 
finances 50% of the project co st in the form of 50% grant and 50% 
loan to SEBs in the case of Non Special Category States. SEBs/Utilities 
have to arrange remaining 50% of the fund from Power Finance 
Corporation (PFC) and Rural Electrification Corporation (REC) or 
other financial institutions as counter-part fund. For Special Category 
States, Government of India provi des 100% of the project cost as 
financial assistance in the ratio of 90% grant and 10% loan. (States of 
north-eastern region, Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, 
Uttaranchal and Sikkim are covered under special category). 
(ii)   Incentive component-The State Governments are incentivised up to 
50% of the actual cash loss reduction by SEBs/Utilities, as grant. The 
year 2000-01 is taken as the base ye ar for the calculation of loss 
reduction. Under this components, funds would be provi ded by 
Government of India to State Governments is 100% grant. This 
component has been introduced to motivate the SEBs/utilities to 
reduce their financial losses. The cash losses are calculated net of 
subsidy and receivables. 
(d) The Government has provided a budget allocation of Rs.3500 crores under 
APDRP for 2003-04 which includes investment and incentive components. 
Release of funds under investment component depends on the utilization by the 
State Utilities. Release of fund under incentive component depends on the State 
Government making claims of cash loss reduction supported by Audit Report. 
The grant component to t he State under investment and incentive component is 
determined as explained in (c) above.

Setting up Rural Electrification (Supply) Technology Mission 
176.  SHRI VAYALAR RAVI : 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY :  
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state : 
(a) whether the Power Ministry has joined hands with the Ministry of Non-
conventional Energy Sources to set up the Rural Electrification (Supply) 
Technology Mission through the decentralized generation system; 
(b) if so, whether the objective of the mission is to provide power to all 
villages by 2007 and to all households by 2012; 
(c) if so, what are the other main objectives of this Mission; 
(d) what progress is this regard has been made; and 
(e) to what extent the villages have so far been covered under this plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) In order to ensure supply of power in rural 
areas by way of setting up small gener ating units (distributed generation) 
based on a variety of local fuels along with localized distribution, Ministry of 
Power has constituted Rural Electrification (Supply) Technology Mission (REST) 
under the chairmanship of Secretary (Power). 
106 

[3 December, 2003] RAJYASABHA 
It comprises members from different Ministries including Ministry of Non-
Conventional Energy Sources and other organizations. 
The main objectives of this Mission are :— 
(i) to evolve a strategy based on technology which could provide for low 
cost power generation and low cost of delivery in the rural areas 
which can be managed by local inst itutions like Village Panchayats 
and NGOs; 
(ii) identify feasible size of generating units for different fuels, which are 
locally available, and for mini and micro hydel projects; 
(iii) suggest type of technologies to be adopted for setting up local 
distribution networks with or without connectivity to the Grid and to 
cover at least 25% of the villages in the country under the Mission, 
and 
(iv)   to access funds requirements for the next two Plans. 
(d) REST Mission has identified biomass gasification, Solar Photo Voltaic 
Cells and generating sets based on locally available fuels as the feasibe 
technology for villages and household electrification. 
(e) Under section (4) of the Electricity Act, 2003, National policy for 
distributed generation (Stand along System) including those based on 
renewable sources of energy and other non-conventional sources of energy is to 
be notified in consultation with the State Governments. Implementation under 
REST Mission depends on notification of the above policy.

GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) The total number of cotton/ man-made

(c) The Government seeks to foster a policy regime, which facilitates growth 
and development of India industry. It has taken a number of steps for revival of

India to banks, amalgamation of sick units with healthy units, setting up of Board 
for Industrial and financial Reconstruction (BIFR) under the Sick Industrial 
Companies (Special Provisions) Act, etc. The Reserve Bank of India has 
been issuing from time to time elaborate guidelines covering all areas of 
industrial rehabiliation viz. detection of industrial sickness at incipient stage, 
identification of sick/ weak units, carryi ng out viability study of the units then 
extending relief and concessions to only viable units, co-ordination among 
banks and financial institutions and ban ks themselves, norms for promoter's

*6. SHRI K. RAMA MOHAN RAO : Will the Minister of WATER

(a) whether Government propose to take up linking of Mahanadi with 
Vaigai rivers early to tackle the problem of recurrent floods and droughts in 
different parts of the country; 
(b) if so, by when the link-work would start; and

are to be taken up with a national perspective, are proposed to be solved? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN SETHI): 
(a) and (b) Ministry of Water Resour ces, then known as the Ministry of 
Irrigation, formulated a National Perspective Plan for water resources 
development in 1980 which envisages inter linkages among Peninsular Rivers 
and Himalayan Rivers for transferring water from surplus basins to water deficit 
areas for optimum utilisation of water resources. Under the Peninsular 
component, interlinking of Mahanadi-Godavari-Krishna-Pannar-Cauvery and 
Vaigai is envisaged. The linking of Mahandi-Vaigai river system has nine 
component links out of which Feasibility Reports (FRs) of 3 links have already 
been completed while field surveys and investigations for preparation of FRs in 
respect of the remaining 6 links are scheduled for completion by 2005. Detailed 
Project Reports of these links are scheduled for completion by 2006. The Union 
Government has setup a Task Force on December 13,2002 with a view to 
bringing about a consensus among the States and provide guidance on norms of 
appraisal of individual projects and modalities for project funding, etc., for 
implementing the interlinking of rivers.

Right to contamination-free water to domestic users 
*11. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY:  
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Delhi Jal Board Act, 1996 does not recognise 
the right of the consumer to be supplied with contamination-free water to the 
domestic users; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and whether Government propose to correct 
this inadequacy in law to give a legal cover against unsafe water supply; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN SETHI): 
(a) Water is a State subject and the primary responsibility for supplying 
domestic water for use by the consumers in Delhi lies with the Government of 
National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi. The Delhi Jal Board, under the 
Government of NCT of Delhi, has informed that there is no express mention in 
the Delhi Water Board Act, 1998 (not of 1996 as mentioned in the Question) to 
supply contamination free water for domestic use as the Act has the provision to 
supply unfiltered water also. 
(b) and (c) They have also stated that the Delhi Jal Board has taken on itself 
the onus of treating the raw water to potable standards at the water treatment 
plants and the water so treated meets the drinking water 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2003] 
quality as per parameters fixed by the Bureau of Indian Standards. The Delhi 
Jal Board has six modern zonal laboratories, throughout Delhi, to test and 
monitor the quality of water supplied round the clock. Random samplings are 
also done daily at consumer end to check incidence of contamination at the 
consumer's tap. Samples are also got tested from reputed national laboratories. 
In addition, these reports are compiled and submitted to various health 
authorities. Delhi Jal Board has stated that the Board is taking every precaution 
to ensure that the water supplied is wholesome and potable and that no 
separate legislation is considered necessary in view of its above efforts and 
effective control on the quality of water.

'26. PROF.M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are thinking of setting up a 
Pension Regulatory Authority; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what are the reasons for setting up of such an authority? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) to (c) The Government decided to 
introduce a defined contribution based new pension system for new entrants 
to Central Government, except Armed forces, in the first stage, replacing the 
existing defined benefit pension system. The new system will also be available, 
on a voluntarily basis to all persons including self employed professionals and 
others in the un-organised sector. An  independent Pension Fund Regulatory 
and Development Authority (PFRDA) will regulate and develop the pension 
market. Consequent to this decision, an interim Pension Fund Regulatory and 
Development Authority (PFRDA) was set up through a Resolution dated 10th 
October, 2003. 
The interim PFRDA is to be headed by a Chairman with the status of not less 
than a Secretary to the Government of  India and would be appointed by the 
Central Government. Other members of the interim body, not exceeding four 
in number, of whom not more than two shall serve full time, shall also be 
appointed by the Central Government from amongst persons having 
experience and knowledge in economics, fi nance, legal and administrative 
matters with one person from each discipline. The Chairman will be from any 
of the above disciplines.

Meeting of Indo-Bangladesh Joint River Commission 
100.  SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY : 
SHRI MURLI DEORA:  
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a meeting of Indo-Bangladesh Joint River Commission was 
held in New Delhi in September, 2003; 
(b) if so, the subjects discussed and the decisions arrived at therein; 
(c) the number of rivers on which disputes over sharing the water 
persists; 
(d) the number of treaties entered into so far; 
(e) the steps taken to resolve the matter in a cordial manner; and 
(f) whether it is also a fact that the Bangladesh Government raised 
the issue of India's proposed project of inter-linking of rivers in the meeting 
although it was not listed on the agenda? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. The 35th 
meeting of the Indo-Bangladesh Joint River Commission was held at New Delhi 
on 29th September to 1st October, 2003. 
(b) During the meeting, under the Agenda Items the Commission 
reviewed the progress in implementation of the sharing arrangements under 
the 1996 Indo-Bangladesh Treaty on Sharing of Ganga/Ganges Waters. While 
reviewing the progress of works by the Joint Committee of Experts (JCE) on 
arrangements for sharing waters of Teesta and other six common rivers 
namely, Manu, Muhuri, Khowai, Gumti, Dharla (Jaldhaka) and Dudhkumar 
(Torsa), the Commission directed the JCE to finalise the Terms of Reference for 
the Joint Scientific Study to assess the availability and demand of Teesta waters 
in each country and draft Interim Agreement for sharing of the Teesta flows by 
the end of 2003 and expedite the formulation for sharing of water for other six 
rivers. The Commission discussed the issue relating to unprecedented floods 
of 2000 in West Bengal of India and Southwest Bangladesh and ways and 
means to tackle such eventuality in the future and directed the I ndo-
Bangladesh Task Force on the Icchamati Basin to come up a timely action plan. 
The cooperation in the flood forecasting and warning 
238 

[3 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
arrangements between the two countries was also discussed and the 
Commission directed the Experts Committee to hold another meeting. As 
regards arsenic mitigation and the decision of the Government of India for 
supplying of the arsenic kits as well as  arsenic removal plants including filters 
to Bangladesh on a complimentary basis, the Bangladesh side assured to 
send their scientists for pre-inspection of the items. India's proposed 
Tipaimukh Dam Project on river Barak was also discussed where it was 
assured by India that if it is ever decided to build and diversion structure on 
the Barak river, it would be done after due consultations with Bangladesh. 
India's proposed River Linking Project and repair to the embankments 
along the Muhuri river in Tripura also came up for discussion as 
miscellaneous items. 
Regarding the River-Linking Projec t, the Indian side stated that the 
proposal was only at a conceptual stage and that there was nothing to discuss 
on this matter. As regards the repai r to the embankments along the Muhuri 
rivers in Tripura, the Indian side was assured by the Bangladesh side that it 
would approach the relevant authorit ies in Bangladesh to obtain an early 
decision on the matter, preferably by January, 2004. 
(c) There is no dispute on any river ov er sharing of the waters. However, 
as stated above, discussions are continuing with Bangladesh for finalization of 
the arrangements of sharing of waters of Teesta and other six common rivers. 
(d) One i.e. Indo-Bangladesh Treaty on sharing of waters of the 
Ganga/Ganges at Farakka 1996. 
(e) The Permanent Joint River Commission (JRC) has been established 
between the India and Bangladesh in the Year 1972 and various meetings 
under the Commission are held in a cordial manner to resolve the matters 
relating to common rivers. 
(f) Yes, Sir. The issue of India's proposed river interlinking project 
was raised by the Bangladesh side. However, the same was discussed 
as a miscellaneous item and not as an Agenda item.

China to divert rivers originating from Tibet including Brahmaputra. However, the 
Chinese side has informed that their Government has not taken any decision in 
this regard.

103. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to refer to answer to the Unstarred Question 1777 
given in the Rajya Sabha on the 5th August, 2003 and state: 
(a) the details of the schemes finalized and achievements made so far on 
erosion protection work of Majuli Is land of Assam both short-term and long-

operational? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKR AVARTY): (a) to (e) Long-term 
measures: 
The Detailed Project Report prepared by Brahmaputra Board, which was 
earlier estimated to cost of Rs. 102.43 crore was examined in the Central Water 
Commission and has been technically cleared for an amount of Rs. 86.56 crore. The 
Brahmaputra Board would be conducting model study of the entire reach of the 
Majuli Island to study the river configuration to firm up the long-term measures 
proposed in the above scheme. 
Short-term measures: 
As regard short-term measures, the Brahmaputra Board had constituted 
a Committee of Experts comprising of senior officers fr om Water Resources 
Department, Government of Assam,  Central Water Commission, Central 
Water & Power Research Station, Brahmaputra Board to identify and suggest 
immediate anti-erosion measures to be taken up for protection of Majuli 
Island. On the recommendation of the Committee, a modified scheme 
amounting to Rs. 6.21 crore has been formulated by Brahmaputra Board and 
technically cleared by Central Water Commission for taking up immediate 
anti-erosion measures for Majuli Island. The Standing Finance Committee 
memorandum, which,

Viability of Desalination Process 
106. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have carried out so far a research to find out the 
viability of desalination process as a proven option to augment the water 
resources in the water scarcity areas in the country; 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2003] 
(.b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what other steps are being taken to address the problems of 
acute water shortage in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Central Salt & Marine 
Chemicals Research Institute (CSMCRI), Bhav Nagar; Bhabha Atomic 
Research Centre and Defence Laboratory, Jodhpur have carried out some 
research work on the desalination process. Desalination is a separation 
process that treats saline water to reduce the dissolved salt content to a 
usable level. The cost of desalination process depends on the size of the plant, 
salinity of water, raw water pumping depth, approachabilityof site and 
availability of maintenance facility, desi gn of pretreatment system etc. The 
water is considered as brackish and not suitable for drinking if it contains total 
dissolved solids (TDS) exceeding 1,500 pa rts per million (PPM). The cost of 
desalination is relatively high. 
(c) To address the problem of acut e water shortage and to augment the 
availability of water in the country, storage capacity of 177 billion cubic (BCM) 
has been created. Another 75 BCM of storage will be created on completion of 
projects, which are under various stages of construction. Proposals for additional 
projects are also under formulation/consideration for creation of storage capacity 
of 132 BCM. To accelerate creation of irrigation potential by early completion of 
ongoing schemes, Government of India has launched Accelerated Irrigation 
Benefits Programme (AIBP). Government of India is also promoting rainwater 
harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water. Central Ground Water Board 
has also taken up a Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of Recharge to Ground 
Water" on pilot basis. For meeting future requirements of water, as a long-term 
measure, National Water Development Agency have formulated National 
Perspective Plan for water resources development which envisages 
interlinking various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers wherever feasible, 
as per consensus between donor-donee States.
